lines: Fever, difficulty breathing, and leg pain following flea exposure at ranch.
This 26-year-old female with lupus, hereditary angioedema, and cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia (hospitalized 2022, 2023) presents with acute symptoms.
Over the past 4 days, she has developed progressive fatigue, chills, dry cough that became blood-streaked, and pain in her left groin.
She also noticed a painful skin lesion on her ankle that appeared shortly after she removed a flea from her sock.
- Hereditary Angioedema Type I (C1 Esterase Inhibitor Deficiency)
- Lupus Nephritis Class IV (diffuse proliferative, in remission)
- History of spontaneous abortion (10 weeks gestation)
- Danazol 200 mg PO TID (for HAE long-term prophylaxis)
- Father: Hereditary Angioedema (confirmed C1 inhibitor deficiency)
She lives with her parents on a ranch in northern Arizona and has frequent exposure to livestock and stray cats.
On arrival, she is febrile and dyspneic.
Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg.
On physical exam, there is a 1.5-cm necrotic ulcer on her lateral ankle and multiple erythematous macules on the lower extremities.
A tender, fluctuant 4-cm mass is palpated in the left inguinal region.
Laboratory testing shows leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia.
Aspiration of the groin mass yields purulent material containing many neutrophils and a few gram-negative rods that grow well at 4 degrees Celsius.
